analysis.one_liner: Bans insurers and federal health programs from requiring prior approval or limiting care that plans cover.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would bar health insurers and federal health programs from using prior authorization and other care restrictions, was referred to two House committees in January 2025 and has seen no further action or cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit group health plans, health insurance issuers, and federal health care programs — including Medicare, Medicaid, and the federal employee health program — from imposing prior authorization, step therapy ('fail first' protocols), or medical necessity reviews on any covered service. In plain terms, once a plan covers something, doctors could order it and insurers would have to pay without first signing off. It would take effect for plan years starting January 1, 2026, and has been referred to the Energy and Commerce and Oversight committees with no cosponsors and no hearings or votes. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Patients whose care is delayed or denied while waiting for insurer approval, and the doctors and hospitals who treat them. Anyone in a private plan, Medicare, Medicaid, or the federal employee program who has had a test, drug, imaging scan, or procedure held up by a utilization review would no longer face that hurdle. [S2][S3]

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits all prior authorization requirements, utilization management techniques (including step therapy and fail-first protocols), and medical necessity reviews on any covered item or service for private group and individual plans. [S2][S3]

Applies the same prohibition to federal health care programs — including Medicare, Medicaid, and the federal employee health program — beginning January 1, 2026, so beneficiaries would no longer face approval delays for covered care. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers lose their main tool for controlling costs, and those costs would largely flow to premiums, federal program spending, and employer contributions — meaning patients and taxpayers would bear higher costs even as they get faster access to care. [S2]

drawbacks.text: Removing every utilization review leaves insurers no gatekeeping at all; the strongest objection is that eliminating prior authorization entirely would raise premiums and federal health spending because plans would pay for more services without any check on appropriateness. [S2]

The bill draws no line between burdensome reviews and legitimate ones — even insurers and patient groups who want prior authorization streamlined have generally sought reforms, not a total ban, and a blanket prohibition goes further than any enacted federal policy. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the gain is real: care gets delivered when a doctor orders it, without insurer hold-ups. But the cost side is serious. Utilization management is how insurers control spending, and eliminating it wholesale — with no replacement cost discipline — would likely push premiums up sharply for people who buy coverage, employers, and federal program budgets. A narrower bill targeting abusive denials would carry much less cost risk; this one bans the entire category of review.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote. [S1][S5]

narrative.text: Van Drew introduced the bill on January 22, 2025, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee. [S3][S5]
No member has signed on as a cosponsor. [S4]
Beyond the referral, the bill has no recorded committee or floor action. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers keep their prior authorization and utilization management systems untouched, since the bill has not moved.

for.name: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to two committees. [S3][S5]

sides.party_line_note: No votes or cosponsors exist, so the partisan shape cannot be measured; the only Republican action is the sole sponsor's introduction.

industries.note: Prior authorization, step therapy, and medical necessity review are insurers' primary tools for controlling spending and steering patients to cheaper options; the bill strips all of them, leaving plans to pay for covered care on demand. Insurers benefit from keeping these tools because they hold down premiums but slow and deny care that patients have already been promised. [S2][S3]

Providers would no longer wait for approvals or fight medical necessity appeals, and they would be paid for more of the care they deliver. Patients and providers are on the same side here, against the insurer gatekeeping layer. [S2]

Group health plans include employer plans, which would lose utilization management and face higher claims costs, likely passed back through premiums. Workers are both the premium payers and the patients in that trade-off. [S3]

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since January 2025, the bill is following the usual path of a lone-sponsor proposal: it will almost certainly die quietly in committee unless the sponsor builds support or leadership elevates it. [S1][S4][S5]
